Franschhoek's Skytram

By: Joy Summers | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A proposed new Cable car in Franschhoek is dividing the town, as the project enters the public participation phase

Unique Selling Point:
Beautiful visuals, tension, hostility and fury and everyone wants to talk, a unique SA tourism town, an unequal society, an election year...the DA about to upset its loyal voters...

Summary:
Tonight on Carte Blanche
A proposed new Cable car in the tourist town of Franschhoek is causing a bitter divide between residents. The developers say this is the biggest private investment into Franschhoek for years, critical in a town with low skills and high unemployment. Those against say this is an underhand project, where the community has only been brought in at the end, and it will turn the elegant tourist town into a Disneyland and the promised 37 jobs is not worth the tradeoff.


Haute Cabriere Wine Estate at the foot of the Franschhoek Pass has been identified as the preferred Base Station, and the top station will be in the Middagkrans Peak in the Mont Rochelle nature reserve, a UNESCO Heritage site. The project will need the go ahead from both Stellenbosch municipality and the Department of Forestry, fisheries and environment. Right now they are in the planning stages and canvassing the opinion of the public, and that has become a noisy and hostile affair with a cut-off date for submissions on the 20th March.

The sky tram, which detractors say is a dressed up word for an ugly cable car, will aim to position Franschhoek as the culinary, wine and adventure tourism capital of South Africa with various offerings at both the low and high stations. Paragliders will be able to access the top of the mountain and hiking trails will be upgraded. But residents in the adjacent exclusive estate, are fuming, believing it will reduce the value of their homes, bring noise and light pollution and a host of other impacts. In peak season, there could be as many as 3000 people using the cableway. Exactly how much revenue this will generate is not exactly clear but
The impacts are addressed in a range of documents on Doug Jefferies website, but critics say the some of the studies are vague. In terms of numbers, the developers say that this will benefit GDP by R215 million rand. But why should Franschhoek be the sacrificial lamb to up the GDP figures? asked Barry Phillips, co- chair of the Franschhoek Ratepayers Association.


Further information:
Eagles, butterflies and plant species are at risk, but the risk can be mitigated according to the studies. But putting those concerns aside the traffic will increase. There is a fatal defect in their traffic assessment, says Barry. He is also concerned about how to get all shapes and sizes down the hill in the event of a fire. They won’t be able to evacuate quickly down the hiking trail. Joe Killian, an electrical engineer asks how Franschhoek which is already at its maximum capacity will provide further electricity and the enormous generator needed to drive the cable car in the event of loadshedding, and who is going to pay? He asks.
Then there is the matter of sewerage which will need to be brought down the mountain in a tank below the cable car. The plan is to process it through the adjacent Franschhoek estate sewerage system. Over our dead bodies! Says one resident. But other residents in the town have voiced support for the project. He owns a boutique hotel in the village and says we need a measured response. But the naysayers were quick to hammer him. For Trish Heywood who runs What’s on in Franschhoek in her spare time, it became so hostile on her site she had to start blocking people. She says it’s a myth they want to preserve the sleepy Franschhoek town feel: “ We lost that long ago” she says. And we have a Woolworths, there is no more of the Franschhoek of yesteryear. She is also critical of the massive mansions on the hill in the exclusive estates. They came here with their Camps Bay houses and they look down their noses at us in the village. Bring it on, says Heywood.
In a lively and tension filled story with beautiful visuals, Carte Blanche will investigate this project, who is behind it, its pro’s its cons and whether the Stellenbosch municipality and the National Environmental affairs will give it the thumbs up.

SKYTRAM FINAL SCRIPT FOR TX 24th MARCH 2024 FACT CHECKED

Voice over 1

Time Magazine named Franschhoek, one of the world's greatest places.

But this small Cape tourist town has been tested by the Gods.

In 2020 lockdown almost killed it.

Then last year flood waters washed through its streets and guest houses.

Not once but twice.

But business and residents stood together, and rebuilt their town in time for a bumper tourist season this year.

Then in February Franschhoek was presented with a new proposal that is tearing at the very fabric of the town. Private investors want to erect a cableway here- injecting an initial R230 million rand investment into Franschhoek.

Justin Truter: Director Franschhoek Cableway Company

You can't dispute the fact that it is going to be the biggest creator of jobs in Franschhoek, certainly within our time

John Van Zyl
You can’t turn Franschhoek into a Disneyland! You can't commodify it by sticking a cable car up a mountain and hope that it won't change the very nature of the village!

James Calderwood
I won't be surprised in fact, if the people that are objecting will see themselves up there at some point to see what all the fuss is about and appreciate the views. I am all for it.

Short music up sound

Voice over 2
The public have until the end of April to make their objections. So this is still the first phase of the public participation process Doug Jeffery and his 12 specialists have assessed the Environmental impact.

Doug Jeffery
At this stage, our specialists haven’t found any fatal flaws, anything major that they are significantly concerned about.


Voice over 3
The base station will be here at Haute Cabriere wine estate just at the start of the Franschhoek pass, and the top station, right in the heart of a UNESCO Biosphere reserve.

There are plans for a curio shop, an all-day wine bar, a fine dining restaurant, and if you are feeling adventurous - a place to launch your paraglider

Link
But what has some locals in a fury is that the developers are hoping to attract 3000 people a day, on this mountain, in peak season

Julia D. Vermaak
This beautiful mountain is going to have permanent lights on it, it's going to have pylons sticking out.

Voice over 4
Julia D. Vermaak and her late husband built their retirement dream in this upmarket estate. But she was shocked to discover in February that her home is right next door to the base station of the proposed cable way

Julia D. Vermaak
I actually was beside myself with anger, that we had not been given the respect of being notified that this was in the pipeline. We would not have bought this plot as simple as that.

Thomas Nygard
The lower station is just over to the right here …

Voice over 5
Her neighbour Thomas Nygard showed how close she will be to a three tier parking garage, and hundreds of visitors traipsing around the dam. From the cable way they can ogle into her lounge and her swimming pool. Her home, she says, will devalue by millions

Julia
Now, of course, that's going to annoy anyone. I am retired and my feathers are all fluffed up, and I walk in here and I think, no, they can't do this!

Voice over 6
But the fury in Franschhoek stretches from the exclusive estates down the main road and into the poverty and joblessness of Groendal. It's where lawyer Wilfred Moses has his legal practice and his NGO. Many of the people here he says, were not informed of the cable car

Wilfred Moses
And for that reason they started completely on the wrong foot.

Voice over 7
He is well respected in Franschhoek, as co-chair of the town’s Heritage and Ratepayers Association, and president of its Chamber of Commerce. He found parts of the developers proposal insulting.

Wilfred
They referred to Franschhoek as low skilled people. That is completely unacceptable. We have in this town very skilled people, highly educated people, people with so many years of experience in construction

Voice over 8.
He is critical of the paltry 37 direct jobs on offer, the 2% community donation and the developers approach

Wilfred
The emphasis is not in what is in the best interest of Franschhoek, but rather what is in the interest of creating generational wealth.

Voice over 9
A key investor in the Franschhoek Cable Car is the Graaff family, who still own part of the popular Table mountain cableway in Cape Town.

Two South Africans as well as a retired Swiss National from the company that will build the Franschhoek cable car are shareholders. The Franschhoek Cableway company turned down our request for an interview.

Director Justin Truter
“Unfortunately, the shareholders have taken a position that we will not engage on Facebook pages, or in the media, while the independent processes is underway”

Erin
We, as Carte Blanche, approached the people behind this venture and asked them for an interview and they've refused us
Wilfred
You're not serious? This is shocking, to say the least! And I just wonder why they are running away?

Up sound James Calderwood
So these are the pictures that we have got…

Voice over 10
James Calderwood is in favour of the project. But when he shared some of the developers' pictures on a local Facebook page, he was lambasted by those against it.

Up sound James
the parking bays behind

James Calderwood
Because they disagreed with my stance on the whole issue I have been called obnoxious, contentious, entitled, a piece of trash and not the sharpest tool in the shed. I decided at that point to switch off the commentary because of name calling

Voice over 11
Calderwood has run a successful establishment here for years. He is deeply invested in the town and sold his boutique hotel so he can spend more time in the mountains

James
We need massive private capital investment coming into the valley and this is a gift quite frankly the way I see it, and if people can't see it I can only put it down to a lack of education.

Music up sound flowers and mountain

Voice over 12
James took me to just below the summit of Middagkrans where the top station will be.

James up sound
The benefit of having people here to have this view that we have here today, I think you can’t put a price on it, it's priceless.

LINK
Being up here the view is spectacular and you can see why people would want to put money behind this project to share this view, but this is also why you can see why people in the village are so adamant people should not touch this mountain, on peak days when 3000 people are forecast to come to the cable car station, I would want to be anywhere but here because it would just be too busy.

Up sound Music

Voice over 13
Former professor John Van Zyl was one of the founding members of the Franschhoek transformation charter and he and his wife are actively involved in village life.

John Van Zyl
It’s not a boost to tourism! It’s purely for the benefit of the cable car!

Voice over 14
He says the cable car will destroy the ambience of Franschhoek with an influx of bused in visitors shuttled from car park to car park

Erin
What do you think is going to happen?
John
I think it's going to fizzle out, I think the people who are trying to get this going are going to get cold feet. I think that the amount of real anger is very strong and I don't think they will be willing to endure that.

Voice over 15
But there ARE businesses and individuals that support the cable car project and at least one of them claimed defamatory statements had been made against them.

The vitriol we were told was coming from this Facebook page, Stop Franschhoek’s skytram, started by long-time resident Elsa Post.

ELSA
I am passionate about town, I do realise everyone has their own opinions and I know that I have upset people because of my opinion and my feeling.

Voice over 17
One business owner accused Elsa of rallying support for a boycott of businesses that were in favour of the cable car

Erin
Has that passion reached the point of threatening businesses?
Elsa
I have not threatened anyone. I have stated I will boycott some stores.
Erin
Have you exercised your right or have you bullied people, because some people are accusing you of being a bully?
Elsa
I think some people could perceive me as a bully. I have enough options, I don't have to support businesses I don’t wish to support.

Voice over 18
As the process unfolds the objections are landing in environmental expert Doug Jeffery’s inbox

Doug Jeffery
The town themselves shouldn't be fighting with each other. They should be fighting with me. That's my job, to take the flak and to put the facts on the table.

Voice over 19
The ratepayers here are proactive. Currently they’re picking apart Doug Jeffery’s reports.

Pat
You have to assume that the silent voice accepts the project

Voice over 20
Their resident engineer says the town has no spare electricity to drive the huge generators and massive motors needed for the cable car. Their specialist says fires on the mountain make the cableway dangerous; they say there is a fatal flaw in the traffic assessment, and both animals and plants on the mountain will suffer. And they question the benefits outlined in the socio economic study. But Doug says trust the process.

Doug Jeffery
Once we get all these comments in we will understand the cost better, then the authorities will decide on that cost, whether it’s worth it or not, if there is a cost.

Erin
What are you going to have if the cable car goes up?
Julia
I'm going to have a legal matter on my hands because I will not just sit here and be rolled over.

Voice over 21
But the project still has a long way to go before it gets approval by the National Environmental minister, and even then it can be appealed. The developers hope to be selling tickets by late 2026. Perhaps they shouldn't hold their breath.


THE END


PROMO ONE

Voice over
Fury in Franschhoek as a proposed new Cable Way divides residents

JAMES
Because they disagreed with my stance on the issue I have been called obnoxious, contentious, a piece of trash as well as not the sharpest tool in the shed.

Voice over
The public have until the end of April to put their objections in writing.

Doug Jeffery
The town themselves shouldn't be fighting with each other. They should be fighting with me. That's my job.


PROMO TWO

Voice over 1
Investors have proposed a new cableway for Franschhoek

James Calderwood
The benefit of having people here to have this view that we have here today, I think you can’t put a price on it, it's priceless.

Voice over 2
But not everyone welcomes the development.

Erin
What are you going to have if the cable car goes up?
Julia
I'm going to have a legal matter on my hands because I will not just sit here and be rolled over.

PROMO THREE

Voice over 1
It's the largest private investment in recent memory in Franschhoek say developers of a proposed new cableway
But critics say it will destroy the ambience of the village

John Van Zyl
You can’t turn Franshhoek into a Disneyland, you can't commodify it by sticking a cable car up against a mountain and hope that it won't change the very nature of the village

John I think it's going to fizzle out, I think the people who are trying to get this going are going to get cold feet. I think that the amount of real anger is very strong and I don't think they will be willing to endure that. Voice over 15 But there ARE businesses and individuals that support the cable car project and at least one of them claimed defamatory statements had been made against them. The vitriol we were told was coming from this Facebook page, Stop Franschhoek’s skytram, started by long-time resident Elsa Post. ELSA I am passionate about town, I do realise everyone has their own opinions and I know that I have upset people because of my opinion and my feeling. Voice over 17 One business owner accused Elsa of rallying support for a boycott of businesses that were in favour of the cable car Erin Has that passion reached the point of threatening businesses? Elsa I have not threatened anyone. I have stated I will boycott some stores. Erin Have you exercised your right or have you bullied people, because some people are accusing you of being a bully? Elsa I think some people could perceive me as a bully. I have enough options, I don't have to support businesses I don’t wish to support. Voice over 18 As the process unfolds the objections are landing in environmental expert Doug Jeffery’s inbox Doug Jeffery The town themselves shouldn't be fighting with each other. They should be fighting with me. That's my job, to take the flak and to put the facts on the table. Voice over 19 The ratepayers here are proactive. Currently they’re picking apart Doug Jeffery’s reports. Pat You have to assume that the silent voice accepts the project Voice over 20 Their resident engineer says the town has no spare electricity to drive the huge generators and massive motors needed for the cable car. Their specialist says fires on the mountain make the cableway dangerous; they say there is a fatal flaw in the traffic assessment, and both animals and plants on the mountain will suffer. And they question the benefits outlined in the socio economic study. But Doug says trust the process. Doug Jeffery Once we get all these comments in we will understand the cost better, then the authorities will decide on that cost, whether it’s worth it or not, if there is a cost. Erin What are you going to have if the cable car goes up? Julia I'm going to have a legal matter on my hands because I will not just sit here and be rolled over. Voice over 21 But the project still has a long way to go before it gets approval by the National Environmental minister, and even then it can be appealed. The developers hope to be selling tickets by late 2026. Perhaps they shouldn't hold their breath. THE END PROMO ONE Voice over Fury in Franschhoek as a proposed new Cable Way divides residents JAMES Because they disagreed with my stance on the issue I have been called obnoxious, contentious, a piece of trash as well as not the sharpest tool in the shed. Voice over The public have until the end of April to put their objections in writing. Doug Jeffery The town themselves shouldn't be fighting with each other. They should be fighting with me. That's my job. PROMO TWO Voice over 1 Investors have proposed a new cableway for Franschhoek James Calderwood The benefit of having people here to have this view that we have here today, I think you can’t put a price on it, it's priceless. Voice over 2 But not everyone welcomes the development. Erin What are you going to have if the cable car goes up? Julia I'm going to have a legal matter on my hands because I will not just sit here and be rolled over. PROMO THREE Voice over 1 It's the largest private investment in recent memory in Franschhoek say developers of a proposed new cableway But critics say it will destroy the ambience of the village John Van Zyl You can’t turn Franshhoek into a Disneyland, you can't commodify it by sticking a cable car up against a mountain and hope that it won't change the very nature of the village VIDEO

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): A proposed new Cable car in Franschhoek is dividing the town, as the project enters the public participation phase
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Beautiful visuals, tension, hostility and fury and everyone wants to talk, a unique SA tourism town, an unequal society, an election year...the DA about to upset its loyal voters...
metadata.Summary: Tonight on Carte Blanche A proposed new Cable car in the tourist town of Franschhoek is causing a bitter divide between residents. The developers say this is the biggest private investment into Franschhoek for years, critical in a town with low skills and high unemployment. Those against say this is an underhand project, where the community has only been brought in at the end, and it will turn the elegant tourist town into a Disneyland and the promised 37 jobs is not worth the tradeoff. Haute Cabriere Wine Estate at the foot of the Franschhoek Pass has been identified as the preferred Base Station, and the top station will be in the Middagkrans Peak in the Mont Rochelle nature reserve, a UNESCO Heritage site. The project will need the go ahead from both Stellenbosch municipality and the Department of Forestry, fisheries and environment. Right now they are in the planning stages and canvassing the opinion of the public, and that has become a noisy and hostile affair with a cut-off date for submissions on the 20th March. The sky tram, which detractors say is a dressed up word for an ugly cable car, will aim to position Franschhoek as the culinary, wine and adventure tourism capital of South Africa with various offerings at both the low and high stations. Paragliders will be able to access the top of the mountain and hiking trails will be upgraded. But residents in the adjacent exclusive estate, are fuming, believing it will reduce the value of their homes, bring noise and light pollution and a host of other impacts. In peak season, there could be as many as 3000 people using the cableway. Exactly how much revenue this will generate is not exactly clear but The impacts are addressed in a range of documents on Doug Jefferies website, but critics say the some of the studies are vague. In terms of numbers, the developers say that this will benefit GDP by R215 million rand. But why should Franschhoek be the sacrificial lamb to up the GDP figures? asked Barry Phillips, co- chair of the Franschhoek Ratepayers Association.
metadata.Further information: Eagles, butterflies and plant species are at risk, but the risk can be mitigated according to the studies. But putting those concerns aside the traffic will increase. There is a fatal defect in their traffic assessment, says Barry. He is also concerned about how to get all shapes and sizes down the hill in the event of a fire. They won’t be able to evacuate quickly down the hiking trail. Joe Killian, an electrical engineer asks how Franschhoek which is already at its maximum capacity will provide further electricity and the enormous generator needed to drive the cable car in the event of loadshedding, and who is going to pay? He asks. Then there is the matter of sewerage which will need to be brought down the mountain in a tank below the cable car. The plan is to process it through the adjacent Franschhoek estate sewerage system. Over our dead bodies! Says one resident. But other residents in the town have voiced support for the project. He owns a boutique hotel in the village and says we need a measured response. But the naysayers were quick to hammer him. For Trish Heywood who runs What’s on in Franschhoek in her spare time, it became so hostile on her site she had to start blocking people. She says it’s a myth they want to preserve the sleepy Franschhoek town feel: “ We lost that long ago” she says. And we have a Woolworths, there is no more of the Franschhoek of yesteryear. She is also critical of the massive mansions on the hill in the exclusive estates. They came here with their Camps Bay houses and they look down their noses at us in the village. Bring it on, says Heywood. In a lively and tension filled story with beautiful visuals, Carte Blanche will investigate this project, who is behind it, its pro’s its cons and whether the Stellenbosch municipality and the National Environmental affairs will give it the thumbs up.
